newsitem.title: BELGIUM: German troubles rekindle speculation of EMU delay.
newsitem.headline: German troubles rekindle speculation of EMU delay.

text.p: Speculation of a delay in the timetable for Europe's single currency is once again stirring in the background, fuelled in part by Germany's struggling economy and an uncertain future for Chancellor Helmut Kohl.

Although the vast majority of analysts believe a timely start to economic and monetary union will occur in 1999, they acknowledge that the next several months will be critical in determining whether their confidence is justified.
There are essentially three areas of concern -- combining economic fundamentals with political brinksmanship -- which have raised the spectre of a possible delay.

The first is Germany's record jobless rate and the negative impact that will have on public finances in 1997, the year budget deficits must be brought in line with the Maastricht treaty's three-percent-to-GDP target.
The expenditure associated with the jobless rise is more than likely to cause an increase in the public deficit and therefore require additional spending cuts and tax increases.

Werner Becker, senior economist at Deutsche Bank in Frankfurt, reckons a supplementary budget of 10 billion marks is on the cards, but politically the challenge will be how Bonn secures such a package given the opposition's control of the Bundesrat, the upper legislative chamber.
"We still have a chance to reach three percent (of GDP), however, given the very bad labour market we should have another supplementary budget," said Becker.

One compromise has the Kohl government agreeing to bring forward its plans for tax reform to 1998 instead of 1999. This is what the Social Democrats want and if they get it they might be willing to roll over on more spending cuts.

Not all economists, however, believe legislation is required. Klaus Friedrich, chief economist at Dresdner Bank in Frankfurt, says German Finance Minister Theo Waigel should have enough options at his disposal to deal with any revenue decline.
A second trouble spot for EMU is the relations between Germany and the southern states of Italy, Spain and Portugal, or what is increasingly referred to as the "Club-Med" problem.

It is no secret that Germany does not want Italy to join monetary union in 1999, and some analysts admit privately that its reluctance has nothing to do with the latter meeting Maastricht's convergence criteria.

The problem is much deeper and revolves around longstanding cultural differences which are engrained among a vast number of Germans. Politically, Bonn would have a much harder time selling EMU to an already worried populace if Italy is on board.

Within an EU context, however, there is Maastricht, and how one gets around this problem -- worsened if countries like Spain and Portugal qualify -- is anybody's guess. One remedy might be a delay, allowing all to whip their economies into better shape.

"Even if Germany convinces Italy not to make a serious bid for first-round membership, and France acquiesces, winning Spain's approval for the politically necessary task of accompanying Italy in the waiting room may be impossible," says David Marsh, European strategist at Robert Fleming in London.
The most vocal champion of closer European integration has said he has not yet decided whether to stand again in the October 1998 general election.
In a television interview on Sunday, the 66-year German leader said he wanted to achieve a successful conclusion of the EU's Maastricht treaty reform summit in Amsterdam in June.
He would then decide whether to stand again.

"If Kohl will not be available for a further term then it becomes much more difficult to push through monetary union," said Becker of Deutsche Bank, adding, "I think until autumn at the latest he will disclose his intentions."
